newsitem.title: UK: Can gov't PFI review answer builders' prayers?
newsitem.headline: Can gov't PFI review answer builders' prayers?

text.p: "Things can only get better" -- the Labour government's mantra in the run-up to the election would be equally applicable in summing up the mood of the construction industry over the Private Finance Initiative (PFI).
The building sector says things could hardly get worse for PFI after years of log-jam created by delays, red tape and heavy bidding costs at a time when building firms were cash-strapped.

Therefore, the government's speedy announcement this week of a five-week review of the PFI rules -- designed to lure private sector cash into public infrastructure projects -- was widely welcomed by the building industry and analysts alike although they have seen previous attempts to reform the system achieve little.
The speed of the review is not so surprising in view of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's committment to remain within the previous Conservative government's spending straitjacket.

With PFI already increasingly replacing public infrastructure spending, rather than supplementing it, making it work is key to getting major capital spending projects underway whether in schools, health or prisons.

Labour rammed home its desire for practical change by axing the PFI chairman, Alastair Ross Goobey, on Thursday. It also scrapped a rule requiring all capital projects to be tested for PFI-suitability -- a long-standing industry gripe. And it pledged legislation to speed up the award of pending PFI health projects.
Geoffrey Robinson, the Paymaster-General, will be in charge of reforming PFI with the aim of establishing a new task-force within the Treasury itself.
Sir Martin Laing, chairman of the Building Employers Confederation and John Laing Plc told a press briefing on Friday he welcomed the speed of the review.
"The way the government has moved quickly is a good sign for change," he said.
Industry's main desire was to standardise the system for PFI projects, Laing said.
"Standardisation will reduce the costs for bidding companies. Also, Labour has scrapped the universal testing requirement which is key," he said.
This move will help the industry and government focus its resources on PFI projects which are workable and large enough to justify the costs of bidding, say industry leaders.
Mike Betts, analyst at Goldman Sachs, said companies could now concentrate on projects which are "feasible".
"Labour is being very practical so far. It will decide which projects will work under PFI or take the traditional routes (government spending)."
In the past too much time and money was spent on projects which were unsuited to PFI, critics say.
Betts expects a more streamlined PFI framework to emerge. He said Labour could use this as a springboard for encouraging more investment into their two central policy areas -- health and education.
"There is a huge need for new school buildings and repairs. Education, in particular, is a Labour government mission."
PFI health projects will need primary legislation before any contracts can be signed. That too has been promised by Labour.

But these health projects do not allow private sector companies to provide clinical services -- an area which skirts so close to privatisation of healthcare itself that even the Conservatives avoided it.
In all, Labour has said it wants to achieve at least the 10 billion pounds ($16.2 billion) worth of projects earmarked in the government's economic forecasts for the next three years.
Analysts think the changes would smooth the path but not lead to a notable rise in construction output itself because much of the new output has already been factored in.
"But it will clear the logjam and create a better framework. Labour wants to show it's not just sitting on its hands," said Merrill Lynch analyst Kevin Cammack. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
